newsitem.title: FRANCE: Boeing concessions insufficient - French minister.
newsitem.headline: Boeing concessions insufficient - French minister.

text.p: France's European affairs minister said on Wednesday that Boeing Co's "last-minute" concessions to win European approval for its mega-merger with McDonnell Douglas Corp were a step toward averting a potential trade conflict but did not appear sufficient.

French Minister Pierre Moscovici said in a radio interview he expected the European Commission, which was due to rule on the planned $15 billion merger on Wednesday, to take a firm line. He said the French government supported such a stance.
"The Americans made concessions at the last minute...They do not seem complete to me," Moscovici told France Inter radio, though he added that they represented "a start to negotiations".

Asked if Boeing's offer on Tuesday to give up controversial long-term supply pacts with airlines was enough to win approval from Brussels, the French minister said: "Very honestly I don't think so, but the Commission is an independent agency, although we have influence."
German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said on Wednesday it appeared the Commission would clear the deal now, and European Union sources in Brussels concurred.
Asked if France was not out of step with its EU partners on the issue, Moscovici said: "We all -- the French, Germans and British -- have an interest in a strong aeronautical industry.
"I think the Commission will be firm," he said. "We're not cowed by intimidation," he added, in an apparent reference to U.S. President Bill Clinton's intervention in the case.
French President Jacques Chirac renewed a call on Tuesday on the Commission to take a firm line on the Boeing-McDonnell Douglas merger prior to the U.S. company's concessions.
Presidential spokeswoman Catherine Colonna told reporters Chirac and Luxembourg Prime Minister Jean-Claude Juncker discussed the deal during talks in Paris.
"The president indicated to Mr Juncker that France wanted a very great firmness on this case, which it considers crucial to European interests," Colonna told reporters.

Moscovici said Europe was not trying to provoke a trade war but to defend its interests. He said the Boeing deal would have an important impact on European's aerospace industry, both civil and military.
